Primary responsibilities of this role include:

  • Planning the project based on a defined need
  • Executing the plan to oversee that the project team completes their assignments according to plan
  • Monitoring and controlling the work so that the project remains on track and in control
  • Closing the project to formalize acceptance of the project result and release project resources
  • Planning for contingencies and report project baseline variances.
  • Communicating with management and stakeholders to enable successful and timely project completion

The person in this role:

  • Coaches the team to drive a successful outcome of the project and the acceptance of the product by the customer
  • Is accountable for the outcome of the project and the acceptance of the product by the customer
  • Is responsible for evaluating a project's risks and for controlling those risks through mitigation strategies
  • Applies management knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to a broad range of tasks to deliver the desired result for a particular project in a timely manner
  • Manages the project to achieve project objectives
  • Controls the technical aspects of the projects
  • Controls the day-to-day aspects of the project
  • Develops and maintains project charter and project plans
  • Executes formal reviews and management reviews
  • Tracks and disposes of issues
  • Helps resolve issues and change requests
  • Tracks action items and budgets
  • Manages technical quality of the solution

While this role heads up the project management office (PMO), the role should not be confused with the PMO function. The project manager and the PMO pursue different objectives and are driven by different requirements. Differences between the two roles may include the following:

Project Manager
PMO
focuses on specified project objectives manages major program changes
controls the assigned project resources to meet project objectives optimizes the use of shared organizational resources across all projects
manages the constraints of individual projects manages the methodologies, standards, overall risk/opportunity, and interdependencies among projects

A successful project manager balances both the "science" of how to perform project management and the "art" of project management, which is learned through experience and soft skill training.

A person in this role needs to demonstrate the following key competencies:

  • Strong communication and interpersonal skills (including negotiation)
  • Detailed knowledge of the project management methodology, tools, and templates (includes project planning, schedule development, change control and cost management)
  • Strong analytical and problem-solving skills

A person performing this role needs the following skills:

  • Leadership and team-building capabilities
  • Thorough experience in the software development lifecycle to coach, guide and support other team members
  • Proficiency in conflict resolution and problem-solving techniques
  • Good skills in presentation, facilitation, communication, and negotiation

This role should be assigned to a single person. From a practical standpoint, it is not recommended to assign this role to multiple people, since if more than one person is responsible for something then no one is. The role may not require a full-time commitment, in which case they may also take on other roles and assignments provided adequate time is allowed for managing the project.
